en: The Treatise on the Profound Fundamental Text of the Great Totality, Scroll One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;
translated by Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
I prostrate to all vidyās without exception, To the stages of the manifold and the non-manifold,
To the single, immeasurable, beyond number and thought, And to all the various classes of beings in the realms of existence.
Fundamentally, there are immeasurable categories of the severing of life; they are equal to the atoms of every dust mote, yet no such phenomena exist.
Furthermore, they are ineffable and non-existent, universally transcending all such dharmas that are neither this nor that.
The Commentary states:
Within these two verses, there are eight sections. What are the eight?

First, the gate that reveals the sovereign of the central-center; second, the gate that reveals the rules of the path; third, the gate that reveals the separation from the mixed and the unification; fourth, the gate that reveals the infinite hair-pores; fifth, the gate that reveals the various ways of being apart from consciousness; sixth, the gate that reveals provisional existence without substantial reality; seventh, the gate that reveals the non-existence of all things; eighth, the gate that reveals the perfection of non-obstruction—these are called the eight.
Within the gate of manifesting the sovereign of the "Middle-of-the-Middle," there are five types.

What are these five? First, the sovereign of the responsive body (*nirmāṇakāya*) that accords with and follows along; second, the sovereign of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) that is unimpeded regarding existence and non-existence; third, the sovereign of the *dharmakāya* which is the fundamental essence and original nature; fourth, the sovereign of the perfected path where both the root and the branches are utterly transcended; and fifth, the sovereign of spontaneous non-obstruction according to response. These are called the five.
In the *Mahādhāraṇī-sūtra on Cultivating the Causes of Practice*, it is said:
"At that time, the Devaputra Flower-Wreath Jewel-Light-Heaven addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"
How many are the inconceivable and non-inconceivable numbers of the First Teacher?

We pray that the World-Honored One will reveal and explain this for our assembly; having heard his names, may we constantly recite and keep them in mind, so that we may emerge from the treasury of ignorance and reach the city of Nirvana.
Thereupon the World-Honored One addressed the devaputra, saying:
"If I were to use my supernormal powers to speak their names throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas, I could never reach the end of them."
I shall now speak briefly, proclaiming the essentials for you, the assembly.
Noble sons! The enumerations of those who have awakened are vast and perfect, exceeding the sands of the Ganges; they are summarized, however, as fivefold.

What are these five? First, the Buddha of the Following Body; second, the Buddha of the Transforming Body; third, the Buddha of the Dharma Body; fourth, the Buddha of the Unfathomable; and fifth, the Buddha of the Responsive Transformation.
Thus it is said at length, and as the verse states: "I prostrate to all the lights without exception.
For what reason are all the Teachers called "Lords" (nātha)?
It is because of three meanings. What are these three?
First is the meaning of sovereignty, for he is the king of all dharmas.
Second is the meaning of being the summit, because the three realms are one;
third is the meaning of pervasiveness, because there is nowhere it does not reach.
These are called the three.
Having thus explained the gate that reveals the central sovereign among the middling, next I shall explain the gate that reveals the rules for the path.
Within this gate, there are six types.

What are these six? First, the principle of vocal resonance, the navel of speech, which is unimpeded, sovereign, and a guiding rule; second, the principle of the fundamental ground upon which all rely, which is uniform and equal, free from all delusions; third, the principle of growth and adornment, wherein each and every thing possesses power; fourth, the principle of ultimate perfection, which exhaustively encompasses all without remainder; fifth, the principle that is neither name nor mark, neither essence nor function, being without fabrication or contrivance; sixth, the principle of spontaneous manifestation, eternally abiding and unchanging, beyond all verbal description, ultimately pure and complete. These are called the six.
In the *Vajrasamādhi-Asaṅga-Vimokṣa-Mūlaprajñā-Svabhāva-Sūtra*, it is said: "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!"
If I were to explain them in detail, there are a total of one billion, seventy-three thousand, three hundred and fifty rules for the paths traversed by practitioners;
if I were to explain them briefly, there are a total of six types of rules for the paths traversed by practitioners.
In this way, these six principles comprehensively encompass the entire ocean-like treasury of immeasurable and boundless rules.

What are the six? First, the principle of exposition; second, the principle of equality; third, the principle of categories; fourth, the principle of supremacy; fifth, the principle of non-principle; and sixth, the principle of constancy.
...as explained at length in the passage beginning with those words.
As the verse states: "Neither one nor many are the various rules (vidhi).
For what reason are all the treasuries of the Dharma (dharmagañja) called rules?
It is because of three meanings. What are these three?
First is the meaning of a gold mold: the seal of the Dharma-gate, which is easily transformed by people of the time, is eternally constant and unchanging, just like that mold.
Second is the meaning of guidance, which leads the practitioner toward the path of treatment, just as a guide does;
third is the meaning of maintenance, which skillfully maintains its own characteristics without loss or impairment, just as a container does.
These are called the three.
Thus has been explained the section on the rules for manifesting the path; next, the section on manifesting the separation from confusion and unification shall be explained.
Within this section, there are three types.
What are the three?

First is the unification through binding: although there is no internal unification among the various classes of immeasurable and boundless ignorance and afflictions that give rise to rebirth, there is external unification, because they establish the meaning of "agreement" (samaya) through their numerical equality and so forth.

Second is the unification through liberation: because all the infinite and boundless noble ones of the three vehicles possess the meaning of unification through internal principle and the meaning of unification through common engagement with the mundane world.

Third, they are fully endowed with the non-union of both, because all the immeasurable and boundless assemblies of great sages within the midst of the vajras are fully capable of realizing the two meanings of the subject that realizes and the object realized.
These are called the three.
In the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, the first of the infinite and inexhaustible sūtras, it is said:
"Although the ocean of the Saṃgha is immeasurable, its fundamental essence consists of only three types."
"What are the three?
First, the ground of rootlessness and non-contention; second, the ground of both roots and non-contention; third, the ground of having roots and non-contention.
Thus it is explained at length.
As the verse says: "Because they are immeasurable, non-enumerable, and non-conceptual, they are one.
For what reason are all members of the Saṅgha called "unified"?
Because there are two reasons.
What are these two?
First is the sense of accumulation, because it gathers together all immeasurable and boundless scattered dusts;
second is the sense of a single type, because it causes all immeasurable and boundless waves of consciousness to settle and abide.
These are called the two.
Thus has been explained the gateway for demonstrating the separation from mixture and unification; next, the gateway for demonstrating the arising of infinite hairs shall be explained.
Within this gateway, there are three sub-gateways.
What are the three?

First, the infinite gateway of hair-like growth of the existent category; second, the infinite gateway of hair-like growth of the empty category; third, the infinite gateway of hair-like growth of the semblance category. These are called the three.
Within the first gate, there are four kinds.
What are these four? First, birth from an egg; second, birth from a womb; third, birth from moisture; and fourth, birth by transformation—these are called the four.
These four modes of birth encompass all the fundamental categories of the infinite classes of sentient beings.
Within these, there are three types according to the intermediate state.
What are these three?

First, the category of emptiness hidden within light; second, the category of emptiness hidden within dark colors; third, the category of emptiness hidden within wind and clouds—these are called the three.
These three categories are non-empty because they are empty; they are empty because they are concealed.
One should carefully examine the retinue of these categories of emptiness; their number is vast, yet it does not exceed this measure.
Within the latter gate, there are also three kinds.
What are these three?

First, the category of illusory transformations, incantations, and arts, which are appearances without underlying reality that resemble their counterparts; second, the category of alchemical elixirs, medicinal formulas, and prohibitions, which are appearances without underlying reality that resemble their counterparts; third, the category of reflections appearing according to their original sources, which resemble their counterparts. These are called the three.
These three categories encompass all the infinite and boundless varieties of fundamental enumerations of similar types.
In the *Saṃgīti-paryāya-sūtra*, it is stated: "The categories of consciousness are, in detail, ten; in brief, three."
What are the three?

First, consciousness is intimately close to sentient beings who exist; second, it is hidden within their locations so that sentient beings are not seen; third, consciousness is distant yet appears to have movement among sentient beings. These are called the three.
...as it is explained at length in the sūtra.
As the verse says: "Together with all the various classes of beings in the realms of rebirth.
For what reason are all sentient beings called "hair-born" (lomaja)?
There are two meanings. What are these two?
First, the meaning of being restless and indeterminate, because there is no fixed dharma regarding rebirth according to one's destiny.
Second is the meaning of being numerous and incalculable, because there are no numerical limits to its corners and sides.
These are the two [meanings].
Now, within this section, it is intended to demonstrate that the noble ones are as rare as horns, while ordinary beings are as numerous as hairs.
Having thus explained the gateway that demonstrates the arising of infinite hairs, next we shall explain the gateway that manifests various [appearances] apart from consciousness.
Within this gateway, there are two types.
What are the two? First, the category of taking life established through collective karma; second, the category of taking life established through individual karma. These are called the two.
Within the first gate, there are four types. What are these four?

First, the category of severing life on the earth-wheel of wind; second, the category of severing life on the earth-wheel of water; third, the category of severing life on the earth-wheel of gold; and fourth, the category of severing life on the earth-wheel of fire. These are called the four.
These four wheels encompass all the fundamental categories and enumerations of life-ending classes established by the collective karma of immeasurable and boundless beings.
As for the category of life-ending names established by individual karma, this refers to the bodies of sentient beings that are not comprised of appropriated matter, such as hair and body hair.
In the *Karmaprabhāva-hetuka-sūtra*, it is said as follows: "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī,
there are two kinds of beings who dwell in the world."
What are these two? First is the general wheel of the world; second is the specific sustenance of the world. These are called the two.
These two worlds are well able to encompass and sustain all infinite and boundless worlds that serve as dwellings and supports.
...and so on, as explained at length.
As the verse says: "And the category of taking life in immeasurable numbers.
For what reason is everything apart from consciousness termed "taking life"?
This is because there is no category of cognition that can apprehend them.

Thus, having already explained the various approaches for demonstrating [the nature of objects] as being apart from consciousness, we shall next explain the approach for demonstrating that they exist only nominally and lack substantial reality.
Within this section, there are five kinds. What are these five? First, existence as a provisional reality like the moon in water;

second, existence as a provisional reality like a city of Gandharvas; third, existence as a provisional reality like the water in a mirage; fourth, existence as a provisional reality like a magical illusion; fifth, existence as a provisional reality like an echo. These are called the five.
The *Mahāratna-ananta-padma-bhūmi-bhūmi-sūtra* states as follows:

"Just as with the five kinds of metaphors for empty discourse, such as the moon in water, [this] collectively subsumes fifty-five thousand five hundred and fifty root names that explain metaphors for empty discourse."
...and so on, as explained at length.
As the verse says: "In each and every equal atom, there is no dharma.
For what reason are all these immeasurable false explanations and metaphors said to be non-existent?
That which lacks a real intrinsic nature is therefore called "non-existent.
Because it lacks reality yet is not entirely nothing, it is called "existent.
Thus has been explained the gate of demonstrating that what is conventionally existent lacks true reality; next, the gate of demonstrating the non-existence of things will be explained.
Within this category, there are four types. What are the four?

First, that which is non-existent like the son of a barren woman; second, that which is non-existent like the horns of a rabbit or a horse; third, that which is non-existent like the hair on a tortoise's fur; and fourth, that which is non-existent like the defilements of an Arhat. These are called the four.
The *Mūla-sūtra* states as follows: "Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha!

Regarding what you previously asked—'What dharma is called the Chapter on Non-existence?'—the four types of fundamental explanations, such as the son of a barren woman and so forth, would be immeasurable in number if I were to explain them in detail."
...as it is explained at length up to that point.
As the verse says: "Including that which is inexpressible and non-existent.
For what reason are all empty phenomena (śūnyadharma) called "non-existent things" (abhāva-vastu)?
Because there are two kinds. What are these two?

First, because that emptiness is the empty nature of phenomena, as explained in these four fundamental [scriptures]; second, because if this emptiness did not express that [emptiness], it would itself be empty. These are called the two.
Thus has been explained the gate of manifesting the non-existence of things; next, the gate of manifesting the perfection of non-obstruction shall be explained.
Within this gate, there are ten types.

What are the ten? First, the primary mental phenomena; second, the mental concomitants; third, the primary material phenomena; fourth, the derivative material phenomena; fifth, non-concordant phenomena; sixth, unconditioned phenomena; seventh, phenomena that are neither conditioned nor unconditioned; eighth, phenomena that are both conditioned and unconditioned; ninth, phenomena that are both [conditioned and unconditioned]; tenth, phenomena that are neither [conditioned nor unconditioned]. These are called the ten.
Regarding the "dharmas that take the mind as their sovereign," this refers to the fundamental natures of the eight consciousnesses and all other mental cognitions.
Regarding the "dharmas that are mental concomitants," this refers to all the derivative mental factors associated with them.
That which is called the "primary dharma of form" refers to the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth that are capable of producing [form].
That which is called the "secondary dharma of form" refers to the various types of derived form (*upādāyarūpa*) produced by those [elements].
That which is said to be "not corresponding to the Dharma" refers to various phenomena that are neither form nor mind.
That which is said to be "unconditioned phenomena" refers to the four kinds of unconditioned phenomena, such as space and so forth.
That which is said to be neither conditioned nor unconditioned phenomena refers to the fundamental nature of all dharmas, such as the single mind.

That which is said to be both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena refers to the functional characteristics of the activities performed by the fundamental nature of all dharmas, such as the single mind.
What is called "both dharma and non-dharma" refers to the first division of the Great Root Dharma.
What is called "neither dharma nor non-dharma" refers to the final division of the Great Root Dharma.

Regarding these ten dharmas, within this present gate, one exists while another does not; one arises while another ceases; one is contrary while the other is compliant; and they are of one category and one kind, never separated from one another. Therefore, it is said that this is the "Gate Manifesting the Fully Endowed Unobstructed."
In the *Sūtra of the Vast Space of the King of Supreme Virtue*, it is said:

"The immeasurable and boundless ocean of Dharma-gates, numbering as many as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakably unspeakable worlds of the ten directions, whether arising, dwelling, or ceasing, are never divided nor ever separated."
"For this reason, it is established and designated as the 'Gate of the Vast, Perfect, Empty, Groundless, Inexhaustible, and Infinite Ocean of the Dharma-realm.
Thus it is taught at length.
As the verse states: "Because it penetrates all such phenomena as both [existence] and non-existence. 2.

The Great Determinative Analysis of the Causes and Conditions for Taking Refuge in the Sphere of Virtue (Śaraṇa-guṇa-sthāna-hetu-pratyaya-mahā-viniścaya). The second section: Having thus explained the Great Determinative Analysis of the Boundlessness of Taking Refuge in the Sphere of Virtue, next the Great Determinative Analysis of the Causes and Conditions for Taking Refuge in the Sphere of Virtue shall be explained.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
Because there are ten kinds of great causes and conditions, he has fashioned an ocean of meritorious qualities as a place of refuge.
What is called ritual, grace, and the application of power, Vastness, excellence, and selflessness,
The certainty of the great ocean and the praise of transformation, Along with the thorough mastery of manifesting one’s own original body.
These ten kinds of great causes and conditions can be fully possessed only by the Great Being;
they are not within the sphere of ordinary beings, nor are they measurable even by the sages, and even Bodhisattvas cannot attain them except in partial measure.
The treatise says:
For what causes and conditions does one take refuge in the locus of virtue?
One takes refuge because there are ten kinds of great causes and conditions.
As it is said in the verse: "Because there are ten kinds of great causes and conditions, one constructs an ocean of meritorious qualities for taking refuge.
What are these ten kinds of causes and conditions?

First is the profound causal condition of reverential salutation and respect: being able to perform salutations and take refuge in the locus of virtue, thereby subduing arrogance and increasing roots of goodness, as the verse says, "Salutation."

Second, by recollecting the causes and conditions for repaying kindness and grace, one is able to compose sublime and wondrous treatises and teachings to enlighten all deluded sentient beings, causing them to rejoice in every source of virtue; as the verse says, "Because of kindness."

Third, one must pray for the bestowal of power as a causal condition; for if one were to compose a great treatise on the Dharma-gates, should those virtuous ones not bestow their power, one would be unable to discern the ocean of Dharma-gates. As the verse says: "and by the bestowal of power."

Fourth, by opening up and widely disseminating [the teachings] so that causes and conditions are understood, one uses wondrous speech and eloquent expressions to reveal the vast ocean of secret, subtle, and profound textual meanings within those various sūtras; this is for the sake of making them expansive, as the verse says: "Vast."

Fifth, he exhorts beings to produce extraordinary causes and conditions by composing treatises and teachings that reveal the meaning of the texts; for if those sentient beings did not take refuge [in him], they would be unable to ultimately believe, accept, and practice them. Thus, as the verse says: "extraordinary."
Sixth, because one cultivates the causes and conditions of patience and non-self, giving rise to joy, reverence, and devotion through a vast mind—as the verse says: "With non-self."

Seventh is the definitive causal condition for the arising of merit: by taking refuge in the locus of virtue and composing this treatise, whether one sees or hears it, or sees the one who sees it or hears the one who hears it, or dwells in the same land—all such persons shall, at all times and without deviation, give rise to and increase immeasurable and boundless categories of all meritorious roots and wholesome qualities. Because this is definitively and unfailingly so, as the verse says: "Because it is definitive."

Eighth is the causal condition of the inexhaustible treasure-trove of the great ocean: by accumulating immeasurable and boundless varieties of all powers, one fashions the supreme and perfect Great Ocean Wish-Fulfilling Jewel Wheel and the Vajra Treasury of Virtue. This is for the purpose of rescuing and liberating the infinite and boundless classes of sentient beings suffering from poverty and affliction, as stated in the verse: "The great ocean."

Ninth is the skillful means of teaching and transforming through causes and conditions. Although there is no separate refuge within those who are fully endowed [with the three jewels], the praise of teaching and transforming is for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, as the verse says: "and praising transformation."

Tenth, he manifests and demonstrates the causal conditions of his own past bodies; because all places of merit to which one returns are entirely encompassed by his own self, as the verse states that he "simultaneously manifests his own original body."
These are called the ten kinds of marks of great causal conditions.
By whom were such vast and sublime causal conditions created?
They were created by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Even Bodhisattvas cannot accomplish this, let alone ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles.

As the verse states: "These ten kinds of great causes and conditions can be fully possessed only by Great Beings; they are not the domain of ordinary beings, nor are they within the measure of noble ones, and even Bodhisattvas cannot achieve them except according to their respective capacities. Thus it is said.
The Treatise on the Profound Source Text of the Great Fundamental Ground, Scroll One.

Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. Part Three:

The Great Decisive Analysis of the Single Path of Vajra. The Third: The Great Decisive Analysis of the Single Path of Vajra. Thus, having already explained the Great Decisive Analysis of the Causes and Conditions for Taking Refuge in the Meritorious Objects, next I shall explain the Great Decisive Analysis of the Single Path of Vajra.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
There is one kind of vajra-ground, which comprises five stages in total.
That is to say: the gradual and the ultimate, as well as the unequal and the equal, along with these five types of stages,
are fully and exhaustively taught within the various sūtras.
The Treatise says:
Within the stage of the unimpeded fundamental ground (*anāvaraṇa-mūlabhūmi*) of the single kind of vajra path, how many stages are there in total?
Although they are immeasurable when explained in detail, briefly stated, there are five kinds.
These five stages are the universal synthesis, the fundamental basis, the central treasury, and the source of all; as the verse states: "The single vajra-ground contains, in total, five stages."
What are called the five fundamental positions? First, the position of gradual transition without skipping stages;

second, the position of ultimate total retention (*dhāraṇī*) without remainder; third, the position of pervasive, perfect, and vastness; fourth, the position where all phenomena are neither [existent nor non-existent]; and fifth, the position where all phenomena are both [existent and non-existent]. These are called the five fundamental positions, as the verse states: "Namely, the gradual, the ultimate, and the perfect; the position of neither, and the position of both."

These five stages are explained according to their own specific principles; thus, these five stages are merely explained according to those principles and do not constitute an exhaustive enumeration. As the verse states: "These five kinds of stages are fully and without remainder taught throughout all the sūtras."
Regarding the fundamental numbers upon which the stages depend, what are their characteristics?
The verse says:
The fundamental numbers upon which they depend total fifty-one.
That is to say, the provisional light, the forty kinds of names,
the immovable true vajra, the ten kinds of fundamental names,
and because of the Great Ultimate Ground— these are called the numbers of the basis.
The treatise says:
Regarding the distinctions in names based upon the five fundamental positions, how many are there?
Although they are immeasurable when explained in detail, briefly stated, there are fifty-one kinds of names.

These fifty-one kinds of fundamental names are the basis for all worlds, all parents, all essential natures, and all supports, as stated in the verse: "The number of fundamental bases is, in total, fifty-one."
What is meant by the number fifty-one?

It refers to the forty kinds within the division of provisional radiant light and the ten kinds within the true vajra; adding to these fifty the stage of the Great Ultimate Spontaneous Dharani, the number fifty-one is thus established.
Within the section on names, what are the characteristics of the forty kinds of enumeration? They are as follows:

namely, the ten kinds of mind of joyful aspiration, the ten kinds of mind of cognitive awareness, the ten kinds of mind of practicing the path, and the ten kinds of mind of non-retrogression, each being distinct.

What are the ten kinds of joyful mind? First is *bikṣata*; second is *amahāśi*; third is *tīvravīrya*; fourth is *haradhi*; fifth is *śamathātiśi*; sixth is *mahā-avaivartika*; seventh is *aravahani*; eighth is *vaimatyāri-rāgadṛṣṭi*; ninth is *śīlakṛśāśīla*; tenth is *mahāvihāra-a-sena*. These are called the ten.
What are the ten types of consciousness that know?

First is *yogācāra*, second is *yogācāraka*, third is *yogin*, fourth is *mahāyogin*, fifth is *ābhasvara*, sixth is *vyavakīrṇa*, seventh is *avyavakīrṇa*, eighth is *vītaśoka*, ninth is *vitāra*, and tenth is *yogācāra*; these are called the ten.
What are the ten mental states of the path of cultivation?

First is *dugaha*; second is *duaner*; third is *dujila*; fourth is *duhodha*; fifth is *dulita*; sixth is *dusavati*; seventh is *dusabi*; eighth is *duaha*; ninth is *dufoa*; tenth is *ducakhiva*. These are called the ten.
What are called the ten non-retrogressive minds?

First is Ratisthala, second is Ratnaśrī, third is Vicitra, fourth is Dharmasthira, fifth is Buddhadatta, sixth is Rakṣasī, seventh is Śilavanta, eighth is Bhaṭṭi, ninth is Brahmabuddhi, and tenth is Dharmāntika; these are called the ten.
As the verse states, these are the forty names of provisional luminosity.

What are the ten true vajra-minds? First is Kumāraga; second is Sūkhaga-īpa; third is Sunāga; fourth is Srotāpanna; fifth is Sakṛdāgāmin; sixth is Anāgāmin; seventh is Arhat; eighth is Anarhat; ninth is Anahaha; tenth is Aharava. These are called the ten, as the verse says: "The immovable true vajra has ten fundamental names."

Within these fifty, one should further add "Bhagavān Buddha" and examine them carefully; this is called the fifty-one types of names. This is because, as stated in the verse and the *Mahāvaipulya*, they are designated by the number of their bases.
Within these fifty-one types of mind, how are their respective stages established as they proceed gradually without skipping over any?
The verse says:
"Among the fifty-one stages, They proceed in succession without skipping."
"One contains all within it; this is called the stage of gradual transformation.
The treatise says:

A single practitioner, within the fifty-one distinct phases of the stages, dedicates themselves toward entry [into the path], proceeding according to their respective order without skipping over any stages.

Why is this so? Because the nature of the stages, positions, and measures of this gateway is such; as the verse states: "Within the fifty-one stages, there is no bypassing or skipping in their respective order."
By what mode of activity does such a practitioner gradually progress? It is by way of progressing through the various stages (*yogasthāna*).
What is meant by the mode of progressing through the various stages?

This means that within the single stage of the mind of faith (*śraddhā-citta*), the remaining fifty minds operate simultaneously, and so on, up until within the single great stage of the ultimate ground (*atyanta-bhūmi*), the remaining fifty minds operate simultaneously.
If that is so, are they a single entity or distinct entities?
In reality, they are distinct entities, yet they are a single entity. Why is this so?
A single state of faith contains all stages, for it is not distinct from other stages.
Yet, while a single state of faith contains all stages, this is because each and every stage likewise contains all stages.
For what reason must one gradually progress through the other stages within a single state of faith?
Because although it possesses that which is possessed within the one, it cannot yet possess that which is possessed within the many; therefore, progression is required.

Now, within this gate, among the fifty-one [stages], all things are fully and completely present; only then is it called the stage of gradual transformation, as the verse says: "Within one, all are complete; this is named the stage of gradual transformation."
The *Mahāyāna-vajra-bīja-sūtra* states as follows:
"A practitioner who walks the path of the vajra turns decisively by means of two great matters."
What are called the two types of decisive transformation?
First, the transformation of universal penetration and thorough understanding; second, the transformation of complete and progressive growth. These are the two.
Regarding the "transformation of universal penetration and thorough mastery," it is because one thoroughly and universally traverses the fifty-one kinds of great paths.
Regarding the "transformation of the complete accumulation of growth," it is because within each and every stage, all stages are subsumed.
Thus it has been extensively explained.
Having thus already explained the gateway of gradual transition without skipping stages, next we shall explain the gateway of the ultimate *dhāraṇī* without remainder.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
Among the fifty-one stages, according to whichever one is first entered,
"Encompassing all and everything is called the ultimate state without remainder.
The commentary states:

Among the fifty-one distinct stages, there are some practitioners who enter by means of faith; some practitioners who enter by means of the stage of the Golden Ground (*suvarṇabhūmi*); and some practitioners who enter by means of the stage of the Great Ultimate (*mahāparamārthabhūmi*).

For practitioners such as these, according to the extent of the stage they first enter, they fully encompass all stages and grounds without exception; there is neither shifting nor transition, neither entering nor exiting, as each and every one is clearly manifest. Therefore, it is called the "position of the gateway of dhāraṇī. As the verse says: "Within the fifty-one stages, according to that which is first entered, all and everything is encompassed; this is named the ultimate state without remainder."
In the *Sūtra on the Inconceivable Assembly Difficult to Enter*, it is said:
"Dedication is then the mind of faith; The mind of faith is then the Buddha-ground;
The Buddha-ground is then the ten grounds. Ultimately, what sequence is there?"
Thus it is said at length.
Having thus explained the gate of the *dhāraṇī* that is exhaustive and ultimate, next I shall explain the gate that is all-pervasive, perfect, and vast.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
The fifty-one kinds of stages are without before or after; they occur simultaneously.
Because they turn together and proceed together, they are called "universally complete.
The commentary states:
In these fifty-one stages, there is no sequence of before or after; they turn simultaneously and proceed simultaneously, with nothing remaining [unaccompanied].

Furthermore, among all the immeasurable and boundless stages within the fifty-one distinct positions, there is no sequence of before or after; they revolve simultaneously and proceed together at once, with nothing remaining. Therefore, it is called the "Perfectly Complete Stage," as the verse states: "The fifty-one kinds of stages, without before or after, revolve and proceed simultaneously; therefore, they are named 'Universal Perfection'."
In the *Dharmadhātu-dharmacakra-ananta-garbha-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
"At that time, having heard what the World-Honored One had spoken, Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, joined his palms in prostration, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"
What is meant by those who practice the path of cultivation without fixed orientation and who turn away from it?
It is as when the World-Honored One proclaimed and revealed such a great matter for the sake of the great assembly.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"It is of one kind and without duality; it is a single path and a single realm.

For those who practice upon the great earth, all paths of cultivation are without before or after; they arise simultaneously, turn together at once, abide and maintain themselves at once, realize entry at once, and are established at once. This is called the 'transversely turning path of the person who has no direction.'"
Thus it is said, and so forth at length.
Having thus explained the gate of universal, perfect, and vast pervasiveness, next we shall explain the gate of the non-duality of all phenomena.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
All immeasurable and boundless, / In every variety of state,
All are entirely non-established; they are termed the stage where both are negated.
The commentary asks:
What meaning is clarified by this verse?

To manifest this gate of "neither-nor," it is neither cause nor fruit, neither stage nor ground, neither existence nor non-existence, neither name nor meaning, neither phenomenon nor principle, neither destruction nor permanence, and neither arising nor ceasing; for everything and everything is entirely "neither. As the verse says: "All immeasurable and boundless, all various stages, are entirely without establishment; this is called the stage and ground of 'neither-nor'."
If that is so, for what reason are these stages established?
They are established as stages precisely because they are not [inherently] real entities. As it is said in the *Mahāvyūha-sūtra*:
"Non-position is the foremost position," and so forth, as explained at length.
Thus has been explained the "neither-nor" gate regarding all phenomena; next, the "both-and" gate regarding all phenomena shall be explained.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
All various phenomena / Are none other than the vajra body.
Because of the meaning of being a single body, it is called the "Gate of Being Identical.
The Treatise says:

All dharmas of immeasurable and boundless stages are entirely the vajra-body and so forth, without distinction; they rely solely upon a single body. Therefore, it is said to be the "Gate of Being Identical."

Why is this so? Because within this gate, there is not a single dharma that is not the adamantine true body; as the verse states: "All various dharmas are none other than the adamantine body; because they share the meaning of being a single body, they are called the 'Gate of All Being. Thus it is said.
The *Sūtra on the Great Earth of Gold Seeds* states:
"A practitioner free from illness perceives only the shadow of the accumulation; he does not perceive the scattered body."

4. The Great Determination of the King of Mountains of the Vajra Jewel Wheel. This is the fourth section, the Great Determination of the King of Mountains of the Vajra Reality Wheel. Thus, having already explained the Great Determination of the Single Path of Vajra, next shall be explained the Great Determination of the King of Mountains of the Vajra Jewel Wheel.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
"Gradual is neither exhaustion nor fulfillment; It is not simultaneous, nor is it prior and subsequent."
"Together," "along with," and "neither together nor not together" occur in terms of identity, difference, time, and place.
The commentary asks:
What meaning is clarified by this verse?

It is because he wishes to manifest that within the body of the Great Powerful Jewel Wheel Mountain King of the Single Body, there are five stages—the gradual transformation of all phenomena, equality, the remainderless ultimate, the all-pervasive perfection, and the simultaneous negation of both—which transform simultaneously, sequentially, concurrently, through mutual negation, both simultaneously and sequentially, and both in one place and in different places, being fully endowed with complete mastery and unimpededness.
In the *Mahāvyūha-kṣitigarbha-ākāśa-dharmadhātu-sūtra*, it is said: "Furthermore, Nāgabuddhi! Regarding what you previously asked:
'What is meant by the Chapter on the Vast Grounds of the Diamond Essence, which are unobstructed and unhindered like the sands of the Ganges, and which consist of constant merits?'..."

Supremely excellent, most wondrous, inconceivable, and utterly beyond thought; the ground of the fivefold vajra path traversed stage by stage; the fundamental self-nature of the inexhaustible inner treasury; the source and the supporting matrix for all that arises and increases.
...and so forth, as explained at length.

Section Five: The Great Determination on the Path of the Golden Wheel Mountain King. Thus, the Great Determination on the Vajra-Jewel-Wheel Mountain King has already been explained; next, the Great Determination on the Path of the Golden Wheel Mountain King shall be explained.
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Within the path of the King of Mountains, there are fifteen stages in total.
Because within the five types of states, each possesses three functions.
The treatise says:
Within the pathways of this king of mountains, the Golden Wheel, how many positions are established as the measure of the path?

Although the detailed exposition is immeasurable, there are briefly fifteen stages; these stages constitute the "Path Section," as the verse states: "Within the path of the King of Mountains, there are fifteen stages in total."
By what causes and conditions are these fifteen fundamental positions within this path clearly understood?
It is because within each of the five types of positions constituting the essence of that Vajra-Mahābala-Ratnacakra-Śailarāja, there are three distinct modes of sovereign activity.
For this reason, fifteen distinct categories are established, as the verse states: "Because within each of the five types of essence and their stages, there are three functions."
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states as follows:
"Within the various stages traversed by the subjects of a king’s realm, there are only fifteen types of substantial entities, activities, and numerical categories; there are no other categories."
...and so forth, as explained at length.
However, the *Vidyādevī-sūkṣma-naya-sūtra* states: "There are twenty-five distinct stages;
these pertain to the transformation of the royal lineage, not to the transformation of the agent."
Regarding the names and characteristics of the fifteen stages of formation, transformation, and inclusion,
the verse says:
"Clear comprehension, distance, number, continuity, and the three unions."
Universal movement and universal immobility, Equality of syllables and the vast,
Pervasive arrival and non-pervasive arrival, Fusion, establishment, and simultaneous transcendence—
These are called the fifteen names, Which should be contemplated in their respective order.
The treatise says:
Within the substance that undergoes gradual transformation in successive order, there are three kinds of functions.
What are these three?

First, one clearly understands and penetrates the functions of the stages (*bhūmi*), establishing the levels in their unconfused sequence; because one clearly discerns the practice and fully comprehends both names and meanings, as the verse says, "clearly."

Second is "far-reaching" (dūraṅgama), because it involves far-reaching cultivation of countless activities; having passed through these stages over immeasurable eons, the accumulation of merit is inexhaustible, as the verse says: "and far-reaching enumeration."

Third, it is the activity that turns without interruption or cessation; because it turns spontaneously, never ceasing from moment to moment and in the intervals between them, as the verse says: "Because of continuity."
These are called the three.
Within the essence of the equality of all phenomena, there are also three kinds of functions.
What are these three?
First, the unification of the signifier and the signified: the skillful verbal expression and the unimpeded wisdom of realization are immeasurable in number, yet they constitute a single vajra.

Second, the unification of the signified and the realized: the profoundly deep ultimate meaning and the supreme, wondrous, and mysterious principle are but a single domain and but a single body, for there are no two divergent paths.
Third is the "conjunction through accordance with circumstances," because all things that possess names, according to their respective circumstances, are entirely one *dharmakāya*.
These are called the three, as the verse says: "Together with the three, they are conjoined."
Within the body of ultimate non-remainder, there are also three kinds of functions.
What are these three?

First is the function of pervasive, perfect movement and transformation; because during the first stage, one universally encompasses all within a single state and proceeds to ultimate transformation, as the verse says: "pervasive movement."

Second is the all-pervasive, perfect, and immovable activity; because that which thus transforms remains constant, unchanging, and unwavering throughout all other infinite stages, as the verse says: "Pervasive and immovable."

Third, names, phrases, and syllables have no distinct functions, as they follow whatever is first uttered and are identical to the others; this is as stated in the verse regarding "syllables and so forth.
These are called the three.
Within the nature of universal perfection, there are also three kinds of activity.
What are these three?

First is the immeasurable, boundless, and vast activity; because the manifestation of the karmic characteristics of its own essential nature is utterly vast and without limits or boundaries, as the verse says: "Vast."
Second is the unimpeded, pervasive, and all-reaching activity, because it establishes all stages simultaneously, as the verse says: "pervasive reaching.

Third is the extremely numerous and non-pervasive activity, because although it universally traverses and passes through [all things], it possesses only one side, as the verse says: "not pervasively reaching."
These are called the three.
Within the essence that is neither [existent] nor [non-existent] and is utterly detached, there are also three kinds of functions.
What are these three?
First, the function of dissolving and not establishing anything: because all phenomena are entirely eliminated and nothing is affirmed, as the verse says, "dissolved."

Second is the establishment that all phenomena possess their respective functions; this is because all phenomena are established as principles through the meaning of "neither [being] nor [not being]," as the verse says: "establishment."

Third, both dissolution and establishment are severed of all functional activity because the ultimate severance of the path is extensively established; as the verse says, "simultaneously transcending.
These are called the three.
These are the names of the fifteen stages.

This path and its stages can be thoroughly realized only by those of sharp faculties; for sentient beings of dull faculties, they are certainly difficult to comprehend, as the verse states: "These are the fifteen names; they should be examined in their proper sequence."

These various stages likewise arise at one time, arise at different times, or arise simultaneously; they evolve in one place, evolve in different places, or evolve in multiple places; they may not arise at all, or they may not shift; and they may be of only one kind, or they may be of many kinds.

Regarding that fundamental dharma, one should carefully examine how there is the application of effort and the application of skillful means, and how it is spontaneously and sovereignly established and constructed.

The Sixth Great Determinative Analysis of the Solitary Mountain King, the Mahā-Śaila-Rāja. Thus, having already explained the Great Determinative Analysis of the Road of the Golden Wheel Mountain King, next the Great Determinative Analysis of the Solitary Mountain King, the Mahā-Śaila-Rāja, shall be explained.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
Within the Great Mountain King, there are in total one thousand two hundred [peaks].
The seventy-five kinds of stages— namely, the fifty-one kinds within the great fundamental stages—
are each fully established through the five successive stages, such as gradual transformation and so forth.
The Treatise says:
Within the essence of this solitary Mountain King, the Mahāśaila, how many stages (*pada*) are established as its constituent parts?

Although a detailed explanation is immeasurable, to state the essentials briefly, there are one thousand two hundred and seventy-five kinds, because they constitute the definitive positions. As the verse states: "Within the Mahāśaila, there are in total one thousand two hundred and seventy-five kinds of positions."
By what causes and conditions are the one thousand two hundred and seventy-five distinct positions clearly manifest and known within the essence of the Mountain King?

It is because, within the fifty-one kinds of fundamental positions that are eternal and constant, each and every one sequentially and gradually transforms all dharmas; these transformations are exhaustive, ultimate, pervasive, perfect, and fully endowed with the five kinds of positions that are utterly free from duality.

Furthermore, because within each of the five stages—such as the stage of gradual transformation—one by one reveals these five distinct stages, there are established one thousand two hundred and seventy-five stages. As the verse states: "Because within each of the fifty-one great fundamental stages, the five stages such as gradual transformation are each fully established."

Within the essence of this solitary Mountain King, the Great Mountain King, these one thousand two hundred and seventy-five kinds of stages likewise evolve at each individual moment, evolve at different moments, evolve simultaneously, or do not evolve at all; they may evolve at the same time in the same place, evolve at the same time in different places, evolve at different times in different places, or do not evolve at all. Being sovereign and spontaneous, without obstruction or hindrance, it is therefore said that this is the Dharma-gate treasury of the inexhaustible, vast ocean of expansive virtues, which emerges stage by stage from the fundamental storehouse of the *dharmadhātu* of the great, inexhaustible void.
The *Mahāprajñālaṃkāradharmadhātusvabhāvakāyagambhīrasūtra* states as follows: "Beyond analogy and beyond metaphor, it is difficult to find;

it can only be described as such: within the ocean-treasury, the great ocean is of one essence; within the ground of the original stage, the three classes of qualities are fully perfected and complete, without any deficiency."
What are these three?
First, the category of superior virtues: the number of their positions and names is vast and incalculable, equal in measure to the number of atoms in the worlds of the ten directions.
Second are those of middling virtue and character; their number and names are equal in measure to the atoms within hundreds of hundreds of billions of three-thousandfold world systems.
Third is the category of those with inferior virtue; their positions and names comprise one thousand two hundred and seventy-five positions.
These are called the three.
Thus, each and every one of these positions continues in this manner, even unto immeasurable, immeasurable, immeasurable, immeasurable, immeasurable, immeasurable [levels].
...and so on, as explained at length.
